plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 35: Geometric Optics and Image Formation
plan.contextChunk: This figure stacks two ray-tracing constructions, panel (a) for a concave mirror and panel (b) for a convex mirror, each drawn in cross section with the mirror as a pale curved arc on the right. In (a) a red upward arrow at the far left is labeled Object, its base P resting on the horizontal optical axis and its tip Q above; the axis also carries the points C, P prime, F, and the vertex V. Four color-coded rays numbered 1 through 4 leave Q: ray 1 in blue runs parallel to the axis and reflects back through F, ray 2 in red arrives along a line through F and leaves parallel to the axis, ray 3 in purple heads toward C and returns along itself with a small right-angle square at the mirror, and ray 4 in green strikes V and reflects symmetrically across the axis. All four cross at Q prime, the tip of a short red downward arrow labeled Image whose base P prime lies between C and F, and a small drawn eye at the lower left looks toward the mirror. Panel (b) repeats the construction on a convex mirror whose focal point F and center of curvature C lie behind the arc: the reflected rays spread apart, and their dashed backward extensions meet at Q prime, tip of a smaller upright red arrow labeled Image standing behind the mirror between V and F. Pairing the panels contrasts rays that genuinely converge with an image sitting only where extensions cross.

interactionPlan.concept: The four principal rays from an object's tip locate its image: for a concave mirror the reflected rays physically converge to a real, inverted image, while for a convex mirror they diverge and only their dashed backward extensions meet at a virtual, upright image behind the mirror.
elements: Horizontal optical axis (thin gray line) spanning the panel
Mirror drawn as a pale blue/white curved arc on the right, concave (bulging right) or convex (bulging left) depending on mode
Mirror vertex V labeled where the arc crosses the axis
Focal point F marked as a small red dot on the axis (in front of mirror for concave, behind for convex)
Center of curvature C marked as a small black dot on the axis (in front for concave, behind for convex)
Object: thick red upward arrow at far left, base P (blue dot) on the axis, tip Q labeled above; text label 'Object' to its left
Image: red arrow at P' — short downward (inverted) arrow between C and F for concave; smaller upright arrow behind the mirror between V and F for convex; tip labeled Q'
Curved leader arrow with text label 'Image' pointing to the image arrow tip

Ray 1 (blue): from Q parallel to the axis to the mirror, reflecting through F (concave) or reflecting away with dashed extension back to F behind mirror (convex), numbered '1' with mid-line arrowheads
Ray 2 (red): from Q along a line through F to the mirror, reflecting parallel to the axis back to the left; numbered '2'
Ray 3 (purple): from Q along a line through C, striking the mirror perpendicularly and retracing itself; small right-angle square drawn at the mirror surface; numbered '3'
Ray 4 (green): from Q to the vertex V, reflecting symmetrically about the axis; numbered '4'
Dashed continuation segments (convex mode) in matching colors showing virtual backward extensions converging at Q'
Small hand-drawn eye at lower left looking toward the mirror
Panel caption label '(a) concave' or '(b) convex'
Ray legend / numbered color key listing the four ray rules
Text annotation reading 'Real image — rays actually cross' or 'Virtual image — only extensions cross'

interactions.teaches: That a concave mirror converges reflected rays into a real inverted image in front of it, while a convex mirror diverges them so only the dashed backward extensions meet, producing a virtual upright image behind the mirror.
interactions.label: Mirror type

interactions.teaches: The individual construction rule behind each numbered principal ray, isolated from the crowded crossing pattern: parallel-in→through-F, through-F→parallel-out, through-C→retrace, and vertex→equal angles.
interactions.teachesDetail: Clicking a ray's line or its number brightens that ray from Q to the mirror and along its reflected/extended path, dims the other three, and shows its rule text.

interactions.teaches: How image position, size, and orientation depend on where the object sits relative to F and C — inverted and shrinking beyond C, enlarging between C and F, and always small, upright and virtual for the convex mirror.
interactions.label: Object distance from mirror (in focal lengths)

demo_steps.title: The concave construction
demo_steps.narration: A concave mirror with object arrow PQ on the left. All four principal rays leave the tip Q and, after reflection, actually cross at Q' between C and F — a real, inverted image the eye can see in space.

demo_steps.title: Isolate one ray rule
demo_steps.narration: Click ray 1: the blue ray travels parallel to the axis and must reflect through F. Clicking rays 2, 3, and 4 in turn shows the through-F, through-C, and vertex rules — any two of them are enough to fix Q'.

demo_steps.title: Slide the object inward
demo_steps.narration: Move the object from far away toward F. The real image slides outward past C and grows, staying inverted — object position relative to F controls both size and location.

demo_steps.title: Switch to the convex mirror
demo_steps.narration: Flip the mirror. Now the same four rays spread apart after reflection; nothing converges in front of the mirror. Only their dashed backward extensions meet, at a virtual Q' behind the surface.

demo_steps.title: Virtual image stays tame
demo_steps.narration: Slide the object anywhere along the axis: the convex image remains upright, reduced, and trapped between V and F — a virtual image no screen can catch.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: An image is simply where the rays from a point on the object meet — if they meet in real space the image is real and inverted (concave); if only their backward extensions meet, the image is virtual and upright behind the mirror (convex).
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Single wide panel (with the toggle swapping mirror geometry rather than stacking two panels), optical axis a thin gray horizontal line about mid-height, mirror as a pale blue-white curved arc with slight thickness on the right side. Object is a thick salmon-red upward arrow at the far left with base P (blue dot) on the axis and serif-italic label Q at the tip, 'Object' text to its left. Mark C (black dot) and F (red dot) on the axis with italic labels; for concave both lie left of the mirror with C farther out, for convex both lie right of (behind) the arc with C farthest. Four rays in distinct saturated colors: ray 1 teal-blue, ray 2 red, ray 3 purple, ray 4 olive-green, each with bold colored number placed mid-segment and small arrowheads showing propagation direction. Ray 3 gets a small right-angle square where it meets the mirror. In convex mode, reflected rays diverge upward/leftward and their backward extensions are drawn as dashed lines of the same color converging behind the mirror. Image arrow is a lighter red/pink arrow: downward (inverted) between C and F in concave mode, upright and shorter behind the mirror in convex mode, with base P' on the axis and tip Q', plus a curved black leader arrow labeled 'Image'. A small line-art eye sits at the lower left looking rightward. Selected ray renders at full opacity and double stroke weight; unselected rays drop to about 20% opacity. Include a short annotation banner that reads 'Real, inverted image' or 'Virtual, upright image' matching the mode.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes_extra: Keep ray endpoints computed from the object position slider so all four rays always intersect consistently at the same Q'.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Toggle between concave mirror and convex mirror: learner switches the named mirror type; the reflected rays either meet in front of the mirror or spread while dashed backward extensions meet behind it; the difference between real and virtual image formation becomes clear.
- Click on principal ray 1, 2, 3, or 4: learner selects one numbered ray; that ray brightens from object tip to mirror and along its reflected or extended path; the specific ray rule behind each construction is isolated from the busy crossing diagram.
- Slider for object distance from the mirror: learner moves the object along the optical axis; the image arrow shifts, flips, and changes size for the concave case while the convex image stays upright and virtual; the relationship among object position, focal point, and image character becomes clear.

authoredContext:
The figure shows a concave mirror and a convex mirror, each with an arrow-shaped object in front of it. These are the objects whose images we want to locate by ray tracing. To do so, we draw rays from point Q that is on the object but not on the optical axis. We choose to draw our ray from the tip of the object. Principal ray 1 goes from point Q and travels parallel to the optical axis. The reflection of this ray must pass through the focal point, as discussed above. Thus, for the concave mirror, the reflection of principal ray 1 goes through focal point F, as shown in part (b) of the figure. For the convex mirror, the backward extension of the reflection of principal ray 1 goes through the focal point (i.e., a virtual focus). Principal ray 2 travels first on the line going through the focal point and then is reflected back along a line parallel to the optical axis. Principal ray 3 travels toward the center of curvature of the mirror, so it strikes the mirror at normal incidence and is reflected back along the line from which it came. Finally, principal ray 4 strikes the vertex of the mirror and is reflected symmetrically about the optical axis.

The four principal rays shown for both (a) a concave mirror and (b) a convex mirror. The image forms where the rays intersect (for real images) or where their backward extensions intersect (for virtual images).

Figure a shows the cross section of a concave mirror. An upward arrow, labeled object, with base P and tip Q is in front of the mirror. A line connects points P, C, F and V, which is on the mirror. A downward arrow with base P prime and tip Q prime is labeled image. It is smaller than the object. P prime lies on the optical axis between points C and F. Four incident rays, labeled 1 through 4 originate from point Q. All four reflected rays intersect at point Q prime. Figure b shows the cross section of a convex mirror. An upward arrow, labeled object with base P and tip Q is in front of the mirror. A line from point P passes through point V on the mirror and point F behind the mirror before connecting to point C. A smaller, upward arrow, labeled image, with base P prime and tip Q prime is shown behind the mirror. P prime lies on the optical axis between points V and F. Four incident rays originate from point Q. The reflected rays are extended at the back with dotted lines and all seem to originate from point Q prime.

The four principal rays intersect at point Q′, which is where the image of point Q is located. To locate point Q′, drawing any two of these principal rays would suffice. We are thus free to choose whichever of the principal rays we desire to locate the image. Drawing more than two principal rays is sometimes useful to verify that the ray tracing is correct.
sourceQmd: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 35: Geometric Optics and Image Formation

discrepancies: Scale/composition: the whole construction is squeezed into a small region while a large empty band occupies the left third of the canvas — the mirror, object arrow and all text render much smaller relative to the frame than in the source, where the diagram fills the width.
Axis-point labels collide: C, P′, F and V are crammed into a ~100 px stretch with overlapping italic glyphs, whereas the source spaces C, P′, F and V clearly along the axis.
The 'Image' caption and its curved leader sit on top of the mirror arc/ray bundle rather than in the open space below-right of Q′ as in the source.

The purple ray 3 (through C, with the right-angle mark at the mirror) is barely visible in the default view — it is compressed near the lower mirror edge instead of the prominent long diagonal shown in the source.
Added elements not in the source: the green rounded 'Real, inverted image — the rays actually cross' banner and the extended caption '(a) concave mirror' (source reads simply '(a)').

Panel (b) convex is only reachable via the checkbox/step player, so the source's two-panel side-by-side comparison is not visible simultaneously (acceptable as a toggle, but the default view loses the paired composition).
evaluation.notes: Optically correct and richly interactive (step player, mirror toggle, distance slider, per-ray isolation with popups), but the default rendering is compressed into a small part of the canvas with cramped, colliding axis labels (C/P′/F/V) and an 'Image' label overlapping the mirror, which weakens its use as a drop-in replacement for the static figure.
action_items: Tighten the x-domain (e.g. clamp to roughly [object-2, mirror+1]) so the diagram fills the frame and the mirror, object arrow and rays render at source-like size instead of leaving a large blank left margin.

Increase minimum font size and stagger label offsets so C, F, V and P′ never overlap (place P′ below the axis when it falls between C and F, as the source does), and move the 'Image' leader/label into clear space away from the mirror arc.
Boost visibility of ray 3 (purple) in the default state — extend its retraced segment and reposition its '3' number label off the mirror edge so all four principal rays read distinctly at a glance.
Soften or remove the added status banner (or render it as small plain text) so the default view matches the unannotated source composition more closely.
plan_action_items: Consider showing panels (a) and (b) simultaneously (stacked, as in the source) at wide viewports, with the toggle only collapsing to one panel on narrow screens.

discrepancies: Axis-label cluster near the vertex is crowded: 'C', 'P′', 'F' and 'V' sit close together and 'P′' nearly touches the pink image arrow / red ray arrowhead, whereas the source spaces these labels clearly along the axis.
Ray-number labels collide: the green '4' and red '2' near the incident rays overlap within a few pixels, unlike the well-separated bold numerals in the source.
Extra green caption text 'real, inverted image — the rays actually cross' and the sub-caption '(a) concave mirror' are additions not present in the source (source only has '(a)').
The 'V' label is placed inside/left of the arc rather than to the right of the vertex as in the source; the mirror band is a thin light-blue arc rather than the source's thick shaded glass-like band.

Panel (b) (convex mirror) is not visible by default, but it is reachable via the Mirror-type checkbox and demo steps 4–5, so only the single-panel default composition differs from the two-panel source layout.
evaluation.notes: A faithful, well-constructed ray-diagram reproduction with correct four-ray geometry, colors, real inverted image between C and F, eye, and right-angle mark, backed by genuinely pedagogical interactions (step player, mirror toggle, object-distance slider, per-ray isolation); the main weaknesses are crowded/colliding labels near the vertex and among the ray numerals, plus small added caption text not in the source.
action_items: Increase separation for the on-axis labels (C, P′, F, V) — alternate above/below the axis with a larger minimum gap and move 'V' outside the arc to the right of the vertex, as in the source.

plan.concept: The four principal rays from an object's tip locate its image: for a concave mirror the reflected rays physically converge to a real, inverted image, while for a convex mirror they diverge and only their dashed backward extensions meet at a virtual, upright image behind the mirror.
elements: Horizontal optical axis (thin gray line) spanning the panel
Mirror drawn as a pale blue/white curved arc on the right, concave (bulging right) or convex (bulging left) depending on mode
Mirror vertex V labeled where the arc crosses the axis
Focal point F marked as a small red dot on the axis (in front of mirror for concave, behind for convex)
Center of curvature C marked as a small black dot on the axis (in front for concave, behind for convex)
Object: thick red upward arrow at far left, base P (blue dot) on the axis, tip Q labeled above; text label 'Object' to its left
Image: red arrow at P' — short downward (inverted) arrow between C and F for concave; smaller upright arrow behind the mirror between V and F for convex; tip labeled Q'
Curved leader arrow with text label 'Image' pointing to the image arrow tip

Ray 1 (blue): from Q parallel to the axis to the mirror, reflecting through F (concave) or reflecting away with dashed extension back to F behind mirror (convex), numbered '1' with mid-line arrowheads
Ray 2 (red): from Q along a line through F to the mirror, reflecting parallel to the axis back to the left; numbered '2'
Ray 3 (purple): from Q along a line through C, striking the mirror perpendicularly and retracing itself; small right-angle square drawn at the mirror surface; numbered '3'
Ray 4 (green): from Q to the vertex V, reflecting symmetrically about the axis; numbered '4'
Dashed continuation segments (convex mode) in matching colors showing virtual backward extensions converging at Q'
Small hand-drawn eye at lower left looking toward the mirror
Panel caption label '(a) concave' or '(b) convex'
Ray legend / numbered color key listing the four ray rules
Text annotation reading 'Real image — rays actually cross' or 'Virtual image — only extensions cross'

interactions.teaches: That a concave mirror converges reflected rays into a real inverted image in front of it, while a convex mirror diverges them so only the dashed backward extensions meet, producing a virtual upright image behind the mirror.
interactions.label: Mirror type

interactions.teaches: The individual construction rule behind each numbered principal ray, isolated from the crowded crossing pattern: parallel-in→through-F, through-F→parallel-out, through-C→retrace, and vertex→equal angles.
interactions.teachesDetail: Clicking a ray's line or its number brightens that ray from Q to the mirror and along its reflected/extended path, dims the other three, and shows its rule text.

interactions.teaches: How image position, size, and orientation depend on where the object sits relative to F and C — inverted and shrinking beyond C, enlarging between C and F, and always small, upright and virtual for the convex mirror.
interactions.label: Object distance from mirror (in focal lengths)

demo_steps.title: The concave construction
demo_steps.narration: A concave mirror with object arrow PQ on the left. All four principal rays leave the tip Q and, after reflection, actually cross at Q' between C and F — a real, inverted image the eye can see in space.

demo_steps.title: Isolate one ray rule
demo_steps.narration: Click ray 1: the blue ray travels parallel to the axis and must reflect through F. Clicking rays 2, 3, and 4 in turn shows the through-F, through-C, and vertex rules — any two of them are enough to fix Q'.

demo_steps.title: Slide the object inward
demo_steps.narration: Move the object from far away toward F. The real image slides outward past C and grows, staying inverted — object position relative to F controls both size and location.

demo_steps.title: Switch to the convex mirror
demo_steps.narration: Flip the mirror. Now the same four rays spread apart after reflection; nothing converges in front of the mirror. Only their dashed backward extensions meet, at a virtual Q' behind the surface.

demo_steps.title: Virtual image stays tame
demo_steps.narration: Slide the object anywhere along the axis: the convex image remains upright, reduced, and trapped between V and F — a virtual image no screen can catch.

plan.keyInsight: An image is simply where the rays from a point on the object meet — if they meet in real space the image is real and inverted (concave); if only their backward extensions meet, the image is virtual and upright behind the mirror (convex).
plan.reconstructionNotes: Single wide panel (with the toggle swapping mirror geometry rather than stacking two panels), optical axis a thin gray horizontal line about mid-height, mirror as a pale blue-white curved arc with slight thickness on the right side. Object is a thick salmon-red upward arrow at the far left with base P (blue dot) on the axis and serif-italic label Q at the tip, 'Object' text to its left. Mark C (black dot) and F (red dot) on the axis with italic labels; for concave both lie left of the mirror with C farther out, for convex both lie right of (behind) the arc with C farthest. Four rays in distinct saturated colors: ray 1 teal-blue, ray 2 red, ray 3 purple, ray 4 olive-green, each with bold colored number placed mid-segment and small arrowheads showing propagation direction. Ray 3 gets a small right-angle square where it meets the mirror. In convex mode, reflected rays diverge upward/leftward and their backward extensions are drawn as dashed lines of the same color converging behind the mirror. Image arrow is a lighter red/pink arrow: downward (inverted) between C and F in concave mode, upright and shorter behind the mirror in convex mode, with base P' on the axis and tip Q', plus a curved black leader arrow labeled 'Image'. A small line-art eye sits at the lower left looking rightward. Selected ray renders at full opacity and double stroke weight; unselected rays drop to about 20% opacity. Include a short annotation banner that reads 'Real, inverted image' or 'Virtual, upright image' matching the mode.
plan.reconstructionNotes_extra: Keep ray endpoints computed from the object position slider so all four rays always intersect consistently at the same Q'.

discrepancies: Label anchoring near the object is loose: 'P' and 'Q' sit ~50 px to the left of the arrow base/tip rather than tight against them as in the source, and 'Object' nearly touches the optical axis line.

The optical axis is drawn straight through and past the mirror to the right edge; in the source it terminates at the vertex V, and V is labelled right at the mirror surface rather than floating in open space to its left.

The crossing region at Q′ is cluttered — the pink image arrowhead, the 'Q′' label, the ray-'1' numeral and the leader line all overlap, whereas the source keeps Q′ clear with the leader curving away to 'Image'.
Ray 3 (purple) is extended well past the object tip Q to the upper-left frame edge; in the source the incident/retraced ray begins and ends at Q.
The right-angle mark showing normal incidence for ray 3 at the mirror (clearly drawn in both source panels) is barely visible in the rendered output.
